samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Arnold DeHeus was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Zachary Miller
sp.p: Well, my name is Zachary Miller, and I'm sitting here today with Arnold DeHeus. Could you say your name so that we could have it for the record?

sp.speaker: Arnold DeHeus
sp.p: Arnold DeHeus.

sp.speaker: Zachary Miller
sp.p: DeHeus?

sp.speaker: Arnold DeHeus
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Zachary Miller
sp.p: And today's date is June 3rd. We are meeting at about eight o'clock in the morning at Alba (ph) in Fairbanks, Alaska. And Arnold is a veteran of the Merchant Marines. He fought in World War II. And we are going to talk about his life today. So good morning, Arnold. Thank you for coming in.

sp.speaker: Arnold DeHeus
sp.p: Good morning to you. And thanks for setting this up.

sp.speaker: Zachary Miller
sp.p: Now, yesterday, when you came in, you mentioned that your time of service in World War II began before you even joined the Merchant Marine. Could you talk about your experience, where you grew up, first of all, and then how you got involved with the war effort.

sp.speaker: Arnold DeHeus
sp.p: First of all, a little history of myself. I was born in Alaska, in the, at that time, the mining town of Flat. And in 1941 in September my sister and I traveled from here to Oakland, California. I was 14 and she was 12. And my mother gave us the money. We split it up, each carried some. And we made the trip from Fairbanks to Oakland by ourselves, just her and I, without any difficulty. The whole trip went off just fine.

It took about two weeks in get from Fairbanks to Oakland at that time. You had to take the train to Seward, and that was a two-day trip, spent overnight at Curry down there. Then you had to wait for the Alaska steamship. And we went out on the Yukon, which later hit a rock down there on the Inside Passage and sunk.

Then when we got to Seattle there was an old-timer around there that knew the family up here. At that time most everybody knew everybody. And he set us up in the Flight Hotel close by to King Street Station. We stayed there. I went on over and bought our railroad tickets and went on down to Oakland.

So then we were caught in the war. It started in December, and I was in school then, ninth grade. And all the time that I was in school down there, I was taking what they call college preparation courses. So I had -- figuring I was going to go on to college or at least that I would get the best education that I could receive. And this is still at the age of like 14.

sp.speaker: Zachary Miller
sp.p: May I interrupt? Who were you living with at the time? Just your sister?

sp.speaker: Arnold DeHeus
sp.p: I was staying with an aunt. I had an aunt, my mother's sister was living there. So we went down to live with them. And, of course, growing up in Alaska you are very patriotic. We always pledged allegiance in the school. And 4th of July was the big holiday in Fairbanks. They used to say there was only two seasons in Fairbanks, winter and 4th of July. So that would give you some idea of how patriotic everybody was in this area and in that era.

So after that, taking those courses, I took all of the math, like algebra and geometry and algebra theory, by the time I quit school. And I'd had mechanical drawing, woodshop, and things like that and building, so I was familiar with working with my hands and with math. And at age 16 they were short of workers. They was looking for people all the time.

And during my summer vacation I went to work in the shipyards as a shipfitter trainee. And my job there was to get what they call templates, lay it out on the steel and then have the burner or the cutter cut it out. And then I would take these pieces and have a tacker tack them together into position so that the welder could weld them. They were mostly small things like pump foundations for pumps or anything that was simple because I was just learning this.

sp.speaker: Zachary Miller
sp.p: You were 16 at the time?

sp.speaker: Arnold DeHeus
sp.p: 16, mm-hmm. And after one month I got a raise up to ten cents an hour, or something like that, and I felt pretty good. And one of the things about it is the tacker in the plate shop where I worked was the mother of one of the guys I was going to school with. And she knew me and I knew her, and we got along real good. And everybody was always trying to help you, especially a young guy. And I appreciated all that and I learned a lot in there about -- I worked there three months, and then I went back into school, which would have been 11th grade.

sp.speaker: Zachary Miller
sp.p: This was in Oakland?

sp.speaker: Arnold DeHeus
sp.p: In Oakland, yeah.

sp.speaker: Zachary Miller
sp.p: Do you know what type of ship you were working on?

sp.speaker: Arnold DeHeus
sp.p: I don't have any idea. I think it was a C class, what they call -- they were Merchant ships. It was in the Bethlehem yard in Alameda, which is just right across what they call the estuary from Oakland. And it was close to some naval housing there. And I think they had some kind of a Navy depot of some sort in that Alameda area.

But anyway, that -- in that three months I had to go back and keep my school going. So I was in the 11th grade then. But at the time I was already looking ahead because I didn't want the war to pass me by. Something told me that I had to get in that war before it was over.

So I wrote to my mother, who was living in Rampart, Alaska, at that time for permission to join the Navy or the Merchant Marine when I was 17. Well, she drew up the papers, had the commissioner sign it there, who was the highest authority in the village of Rampart at the time, and sent it down to me so I had that prior to my 17th birthday.

So when I rolled around 17, I went down to see the Navy. And the Navy said, yeah, we are looking for you. They sent me over to have a physical in San Francisco. I passed the physical. And I got back to the recruiting office on the Oakland side, and this young fella told me that they would have to contact my mother to verify this. And of course this is April -- by that time it was probably around April.

And I said, "You know, you don't know what you are saying because it's breakup time in Alaska and the only way to get in there is airplane and you can't land the plane because the snow is starting to break up. The river is still halfway full, so you can't -- and thawing, so you can't go on the river because of the ice. So there's just very little chance that that's going to get in there. You are talking a big job to try to get that communication and have her verify it."

I said, "This is signed by the commissioner in the City of Rampart. That's the highest authority you can get there." Well, I'd say typical military training, they do what they're told, regardless of what happens. You don't think what for yourself; you do what you are told. I was pretty upset about that.

And I waited around for a month or so. And you know the young people, at 17 a month can be like a year or two. So I decided that -- I talked it over with somebody else, I think it was, that told me, "Well, the Merchant Marine will take you." I said, "Oh." So I said okay. I went over to San Francisco again and saw the Merchant Marine office. And they said, "Sure. You get ready and get your bags packed and report next week." I said, "You just got a candidate."

I signed everything up there. And they sent me down to Catalina Island right out of Long Beach down there to take my training through the Maritime Service. The Government was running some sort of -- So you didn't go on a ship. I was totally ignorant of fore and aft and top side and lower deck and this type of thing and passageway. You had to learn the nomenclature and take training. So we went down there -- or I did -- and it was about five weeks or six weeks something like that. And they put us through how to survive swimming through the fire. We had to jump off of a 30-foot tower there off the dock with life jackets on.

sp.speaker: Zachary Miller
sp.p: So this was your boot camp training?

sp.speaker: Arnold DeHeus
sp.p: You could call it -- I guess the Navy or Army would call it boot camp. When we were down there, then, you had a choice of the department you wanted to serve in. I chose engine room because I was more prone to wanting to do something that would help me when I got back ashore and the war was over.

And I thought engine room service would be good because everything is -- a ship is just like a little city. Everything that you learn on there would be adaptable to shore. So while I was down there I also took an extra course. They said if you took this course you could get an extra $10 a month, and that was to be a lifeboatman. So I took that course and had my lifeboatman endorsement. That entitled you to be in charge of the lifeboat if you ever were sunk.

So you actually, in a sense, would have the same authority as the captain or officer or anybody else. You were qualified to man that lifeboat and be in charge of it. So I thought that was pretty good for a 17-year-old kid. I thought -- of course, that pumps you up a little bit, gets you excited. The $10 I think had as much to do with it as anything.

sp.speaker: Zachary Miller
sp.p: Right. It was more the honor.

sp.speaker: Arnold DeHeus
sp.p: Yeah. When we started -- when I got my first ship, then, out of San Francisco, it was a tanker. The name of it was the SS Idaho Falls, T-2 type tanker. I think it was probably built -- maybe in the Richmond shipyards they were building those. But it was -- the Navy operated them and also these companies, they sailed them. They had a crew probably of about 40 people, somewhere in that neighborhood.

And then they had armed guard on them. There was about -- I don't know exactly how many, but I would say maybe 20 armed guard. Their armament was a 3-inch 50 in the bow and a 5-inch 38 cannon in the stern and then probably a couple of gun turrets, 20-millimeter around the bridge, two on each side of the bridge, and I think they had two or four 20-millimeter on the stern. And that was their armament for going.

When they first started the war, the Merchant ships were sailing primarily out of the Atlantic to Europe and Russia with material. They traveled unarmed, the early, like in '39, '40, '41 era, hauling especially the supplies to Murmansk. They lost -- it was like going in a shooting gallery. The submarines were even sinking Merchant ships right off the Coast, the East Coast.

sp.speaker: Zachary Miller
sp.p: Were these Japanese subs?

sp.speaker: Arnold DeHeus
sp.p: No, German.

sp.speaker: Zachary Miller
sp.p: German subs. Oh, you're talking on the East Coast.

sp.speaker: Arnold DeHeus
sp.p: East Coast. Murmansk is the northern -- the northernmost ice-free port that I think Russia has. So they were sailing the material into there to supply them. But they weren't armed, and they were just -- they didn't go very fast, you know, so they were like easy targets. Like shooting fish in a barrel for the German submarines. So the Merchant seamen probably lost as much -- at least as much or more per capita as the Marine Corps in World War II.

sp.speaker: Zachary Miller
sp.p: So tell me about your first assignment after boot camp. It was to the SS Idaho Falls?

sp.speaker: Arnold DeHeus
sp.p: Idaho Falls, tanker. And went out as a wiper. And the wiper is lowest rating in the engine room. It would be equivalent to ordinary seaman on a deck. But the thing was -- the good thing about it, you weren't restricted on if you wanted to learn. So the -- and everybody there was willing to help you learn. You could pick their brain every day.

And I was on that ship for eight months, and by the time I got off I could do most of -- a lot of those jobs, like the fireman and oiler's job. They even let me practice with the -- The T-2s were what they call turbo electric. And what they did is they had a big motor that run the propulsion, the shaft and the screw, and they had two generators that supplied the electricity for this big motor. And so they had as much speed backwards as they did forwards -- or as much power, I would say, rather than speed.

But you had to switch the polarity, so they had a great big bar to do that. When we were maneuvering, they would send down a bell that they wanted to go so fast, that they wanted to go reverse, they want to do that. When they do that, then you have to switch it out of this one, switch the polarity on it, push the lever in so you get, like the rheostat, you get the juice to the motor and turn the rpm's. So that was a new thing that they come out with because I got in later, 1944, so they had already made a lot of progress and doing a lot of these more modern ships. The old Libertys were old reciprocating jobs. So we traveled on that trip about 75,000 miles.

sp.speaker: Zachary Miller
sp.p: What port was the Idaho Falls out of?

sp.speaker: Arnold DeHeus
sp.p: Well, it is -- it was out of here. What port do you mean?

sp.speaker: Zachary Miller
sp.p: Yeah. Out of Oakland or --

sp.speaker: Arnold DeHeus
sp.p: San Francisco, yeah. They're right across the bay there. So they had Army docks there, you know, for ships sailing out of there. This one got out of San Francisco. But that was probably the most memorable because we traveled so far that -- and saw so many things, were on the go all the time. And the tanker is easy to load and easy to off-load, in the respect. You don't have to have the winches and take things out of the hold and swing them over. And so you have just pumping to do.

sp.speaker: Zachary Miller
sp.p: Where exactly did you go?

sp.speaker: Arnold DeHeus
sp.p: Well, I don't think my memory is going to remember everything. But to start out with, we hit Honolulu first and went right into that harbor where they made the attack. You go right by Pearl Harbor. It's just across the bay there. The mast of the Arizona was still sticking up. All the damage was still there. So we saw all this as we went in. And we were only there a short time.

I think maybe what they did is -- when we sailed, we didn't know where we were going at that time. The war was still on. So you just got on a ship, and wherever it went, that's where you went. And you didn't know where it was going to go. But we stopped there. And then we went down to Melbourne, Australia. And I think what it was we off-loaded there, and then we went up into the Persian Gulf to pick up another load.

And then one thing about that is they don't realize how hot that area is. I mean, we think it's hot now for war again, but to go in there weather-wise, we were taking sea temperature there. Every hour you took sea temperature, all your temperatures. When we went into the Straits of Hormuz, it jumped seven degrees in one hour. So that showed you that Persian Gulf is a hot spot. That's the only place I remember seeing sea snakes, big long snakes at least as long as ten feet I'd say.

When we got in there to tie up, one of the things that we did for recreation was lower the lifeboat and improvise a flat board, like a surfboard, to drag behind the lifeboat. I didn't have nerve enough to go in with those snakes. Some of those fellas did, but I said, "No. I'll stay here and watch you." That was my first experience with the religion in that area.

As they were working on the ship, dockworkers were Muslims. When their time came for their prayer, they just shut down. War or no war, they shut down and did whatever they had to do. I remember watching them prepare for it. They washed their hands and face and whatever it was and brushed their teeth and whatever they did, spread a mat out. And that was my first experience over there. The other thing was there was no shore leave in that area. You stayed on the ship all the time. So then we came back out of there. And I don't know what order it would be in, but I hit every major port in India and not necessarily on that trip.

I think we went from there back to Calcutta and Madras and Ceylon at that time -- I think it's Sri Lanka now -- then back down to Sydney. And then we went up into the islands up there, New Guinea and someplace around there. I forget what it was. And I've been to all those islands -- Guam and Saipan and Tinian and Eniwetok, Ulithi. And then we started back from there to the Panama Canal.

sp.speaker: Zachary Miller
sp.p: Did you give a date for this? Is this 1933 or --

sp.speaker: Arnold DeHeus
sp.p: No, no.

sp.speaker: Arnold DeHeus
sp.p: No. It would have been from 1944 -- it would have been that latter part of 1944.

sp.speaker: Zachary Miller
sp.p: So September, October?

sp.speaker: Arnold DeHeus
sp.p: Yeah, like -- well, we left in July around, I think I signed on, so it would have to be July, August, and September, somewhere in that three-month frame. And then we took off for the Panama Canal.

sp.speaker: Zachary Miller
sp.p: So the war in Europe was over at this time. Is that --

sp.speaker: Arnold DeHeus
sp.p: No. It wasn't -- Let's see. Well, it wasn't over yet because they just had D-Day in '44. That was in June. So they were still fighting over there. The war was probably over the next spring in '45, and the Japanese surrendered in August of '45.

So what they -- in traveling back across the Pacific we had to rescue a ship. They had burned tubes out of their boilers and they didn't have any propulsion. So we stopped and hooked onto them and took them into the nearest safe port, which happened to be Nuku Hiva in Marquesas Islands. Then we stayed there for a few days till the captains got things straightened out on whatever they were going to do. And then we left there. When we rescued that ship, there were -- they had the whole stern lined with sharks.

The sharks were just all over the place there. And we caught about -- I think they had something like over 50 or up to 60 sharks. And while we were there, we had to slow and just kind of float close to them until the captains signalled back and forth on what we were going to do, how we were going to hook up to that ship. And the first pass that he tried on it, it tore a lifeboat off. I forget if it was ours or theirs, but he was going too fast, too close, and this big lifeboat was ripped right off.

So then we made another pass and they finally got it hooked up. And we got I think a cable on them and a couple of (hoses) stretched out. And there was probably about three, four hundred feet between the two ships. And we towed them. We towed them for a day or two, anyway, because it wasn't that close -- there's not much in the Equator in the Pacific. So then we went on to the Panama Canal, went through there and saw where they had taken some aircraft through, an aircraft carrier. And this carrier -- I forget which one it was -- it got so far this way it knocked the lights down on the side of the Canal because it was just -- it would barely fit in the locks. And it was designed wide for that deck, and the lights went. But they got it through there.

And then we went on to Aruba. And from Aruba it seemed to me we picked up some planes, a deck load of P-51s and P-47s. And then we went across the Atlantic in a convoy. And it was miserable. We are back in the wintertime now. It's probably December time. And the convoy can only go as fast as the slowest ship. They had Liberty ships in there, so we were doing about eight knots.

Well, eight knots is roughly 10 miles an hour. So you can imagine, it's almost just floating like this and not making any headway. Well, we finally got word that -- it was stormy and dark most of the time, overcast. And we got word after a few days that they were sinking the ships, the submarines were. And the word came out to just go as fast as you can and go to your destination. So we headed to Liverpool, England, with that load.

Then we went from there back around through the Mediterranean through the Suez Canal and back to the Gulf again to pick up another load. Then we came back again and over into Le Havre, France -- no, Naples -- Naples, Italy. They were still fighting in the boot up there, I think. We were there about Christmastime, I'm pretty sure of that, because -- not only that, in the wintertime that Mediterranean is not a pleasant trip. It gets rough in there and cold -- or it was when we went through it. And Naples, I'll never forget, the Italians were having a tough time. They weren't prisoners; they were civilians working on the docks. And they were having a tough time with everything.

There was no food -- you know, a little bit. And they hadn't got anything organized. It was still military. But anyway, we had a bunch of that cheap Christmas candy -- I don't know, that sugar kind with the centers in it. They gave us three or four boxes. Well, there wasn't anybody on the ship liked that. So one guy on there, young kid -- we were all kids, I guess, all young -- but one of them started taking his candy and threw it on the dock. And these people hadn't seen any of that stuff, anything sweet, for four or five years. Boy, they were out there picking up the candy, putting it in their pockets to take it home. Some of them ate it right there. Pretty soon, you could see up the dock -- there were other ships there -- here they come, all those workers come running down to the ship we were at because something was going on and handing out something.

And I'll never forget this. Big guy, tall fella, military guy from South Africa -- he had it on his sleeve -- and he was down there on the dock and just cussing us out because he was trying to get those workers to do something and we had them down there. And then this ornery kid, he threw a handful of candy at him. I think if that fella could have got ahold of him he would have really worked us over because it was -- it was a silly thing to do, but when you are at sea a long time and the same old routine, I think a lot of the guys do silly things sometimes.

You look back on it and say, well, it wasn't the right thing to do, but it was -- at the time, it was something, you know, different. So then we went -- from there I think we went to Le Havre in France. And we did get ashore there for a while because they had already gone through there. There still wasn't much there. Everything was still devastation and hadn't recouped yet. It was just that I could say I had been to France. So as near as I can remember, then we went back to the U.S. I'm trying to think of how that trip went.

But I finally, after eight months -- in March we paid off in Port Arthur, Texas. And then I -- what they did is after you were on a trip like that, you could have 30 days ashore. But after 30 days, if you didn't get back to sea again, they would draft you into the Army, because they had to have though those Merchant ships deliver those supplies.

So from Port Arthur I took the -- I think I took the bus back to San Francisco because I wanted to see my relatives there, my sister and other people that I knew. When they paid you off of those ships, they paid you off in cash. They have all the bills lined up. They have like five-hundreds, one-hundreds, fifties, twenties. And You had your payroll slip there. You just give it to the paymaster, he would look up your name, count the money out right there. That was part of the agreement. I forgot to mention that the ship I was on was a union-operated ship, so you joined the union at the same time.

So I was in the Sailors Union of the Pacific at that time. I think it's all joined together and it's called Seafarers International Union. And that's what they called it on the East Coast and the Gulf Coast. So even though they gave us uniforms in our training, you didn't wear uniforms on the ship. You are dressed in civilian clothes. And at that time it's like all the young kids, the period there dressing was engineer boots, Levis, and one of the bomber jackets, and a T-shirt. That was it, the in thing. And that was our -- really our dressiest outfit. We didn't have --
[END OF SIDE ONE, TAPE ONE; BEGIN SIDE TWO, TAPE ONE]

sp.speaker: Zachary Miller
sp.p: We just had to flip the tape over. You were talking about your dress, how you guys -- what kind of clothes you guys would wear on the ship.

sp.speaker: Arnold DeHeus
sp.p: So after my 30 days there -- I think it was on that trip, too, that -- I had some relatives in Santa Cruz California, so I stopped, got off the bus there. You could do that and then pick up your -- on the bus again because you had a ticket that went through to Oakland. So I stopped off there to visit those relatives.

I hadn't seen them in over a year, probably, and talked to them. Well, there was some of the girls, they were like cousins, but it was by marriage, so it was -- and then they got word that I had just got off the ship. And I think that the older people there, you know, in some way or another got word out that I had $600 cash money. They was going to take me down to the -- they had a big, oh, like -- I don't know what you call it -- it was a midway or something, roller coaster and, you know, the carnival, like they have on the beaches, all of those little games and rides and this. So they were going to take me down there and spend my money.

So what I did is I just didn't say anything, I went down and got on an early bus and just pulled out of there and went on to Oakland. I wasn't going to get trapped in that one after working all that time for that money. So then I spent my 30 days up there with the family, visiting.

And the next ship I caught out of there was a Victory ship, and I caught that out of San Francisco again. It was the SS Clovis Victory, C-L-O-V-I-S. And it was another modern ship, but it was a cargo ship. And I went out on that as a fireman because I had learned enough to go up and get another endorsement. So I moved up from wiper to fireman -- or actually fireman/water tender. And so that one took off. And so this would have been like in about the end of April or first of May of 1945.

And I didn't know what the cargo was, and I didn't know where we were going. But as it ended up, we were going to Okinawa, eventually. The invasion took place I think on Easter Sunday or somewhere around there of that year, which happened to be in April. So it was probably around the end of April. We had a load of fog oil on in 55-gallon drums on this Victory ship. And the Victory ship, it's different than the T-2. The T-2 is what they call turbo-electric. This was a steam -- I can't come to mind now, but it was a steam-driven propulsion system, anyway, with what they call a double reduction deal. And the steam went into one unit that turned around -- it would be like fuel to a jet engine -- and then exhausted into another one that turned so that both of those, even though you had low pressure steam after -- turbine electric -- or turbine-driven, I should say. So that was the newer deal.

And those boilers operate at high pressure on both ships. They were like 450 pounds pressure and 750 degrees superheat. So they were up-to-date, latest type of boiler, everything, and higher pressure. The old Libertys operated something like 125 pounds pressure or 150. I think that's about what they are.

Anyway, this load of fog oil had to get to Okinawa in a hurry. So we just bee-lined it to Saipan. And when we got to Saipan, they wanted this so bad in that harbor that they gave us four destroyers to escort us in there. And normally when you are in the war zone, you zigzag so the submarines couldn't get a bead on you. The destroyers that they gave us were so fast, they just kept circling us. And they went full steam ahead, and they just run a circle around us to protect us.

That was one time we had -- it was about a three-day trip, I think, something like that into there. So we had a little contest going to see who could go the fastest on the least amount of fuel. And we were getting at that time -- I think the fastest we got was 22 knots out of that Victory, which would put you up to at least over 25 miles an hour compared to like the eight knots in a convoy. So we were -- we were what they call boogeying it. We were moving out. Well, they got us to Okinawa, and we got in the line. There was no docks or anything there, so you anchored out in what they call the line. And they had a series of these ships. They had like the first line closest to the beach, second line, third line. We were in the farthest line out, same row as the battleships were. And, I don't know, probably several miles away they had -- I think the Texas and the Iowa were there, shelling over there, wherever they were shooting at ashore.

But in the engine room it was enough to get your attention because every time they would fire a salvo, it would travel through that water, and it was like somebody hitting the outside of that ship with a big hammer. It would just go clank, and our pipes would vibrate under there and the dust -- the asbestos would come off. And so -- but you got used to it. You just figured if your time is up, it's up. That's all. And it was -- I say fortunate for us, but unfortunate for every ship around us got hit with kamikazes.

The gunners on our ship -- there was one guy -- I wish I knew who he was -- on a 20-millimeter. Uncanny. He could just -- because I was watching all this action, and the tracers were going right into these kamikazes and they never made it. So he got credit for shooting down two or three of those. But one that he -- that didn't get to us dove right into the hold of a Liberty ship. And I saw cargo and the stevedore -- usually they had Army people on there offloading -- I seen him come flying out of that hole.

We were anchored there 27 days and had over 60 kamikaze air raids in that period of time. So this suicide bombers is nothing new to World War II veterans that were involved with the kamikazes. That just a flying bomb is what it was. There's no -- or a guided missile, if you want to look at it that way. But anyway, this fog oil that we carried and why it was so important, they used on these little ships that run around the harbor, little boats they called them. And they were gun boats. They were armed with 20-millimeter weapons. And they also did the fogging.

They would light this stuff off, and it would fog the harbor out, just like you had big clouds laying there so the kamikazes couldn't see you. The only problem was in the engine room, your air intakes up there would suck that down in that thing. And when they fogged out the harbor, you even had a coat of this oil -- you could feel it on your skin, your face and in your hair, everything. It was fine, and it would lay down there. It would eventually dissipate. And it did have an odor to it. So it was -- it wasn't something you couldn't tolerate, but you knew what it was.

Anyway, the reason we were there so long is they had to offload this six barrels at a time into these what they call the ducks. You see these little ducks, they go in the water and then they'll run right up on land. They are wheel-operated. They have a little screw in the back there. But they don't have any freeboard. They might have about -- I think what they were doing was maybe six inches of free board or something like that. And one time one of them was heading ashore with a load, and one of these other boats had to go someplace and they were zipping by there creating a pretty good wake.

And this duck just went up to the crest of the wave and went back down into the trough and just kept going right to the bottom. That was something. Here the barrels were floating, and guys were floating out there. They rescued them right away, but that was my experience with this business of watching them.

Well, we were there so long that we wanted to get ashore. You could still hear them fighting and firing and everything up there, but we wanted to get ashore and walk on land and say that we'd been on Okinawa. So we bummed a ride on one of these ducks and went ashore. I think there was two or three of us, something like that. So we got ashore. And we were out there in our civilian clothes, mind you, like I told you. And pretty soon one of these Army trucks with some GIs in it stopped and give us a ride. They all had their weapons on. I think they call them a six-by-six, their truck. We got in the back end. It had a big bed on it. So they took us up there a little ways. We wanted to go to the front. They said, "No, you don't want to go to the front. If you get up there and you are not attached to anything, they are going to grab you and put you on grave detail -- or body detail."

You'd go out and pick up the bodies and bring them in. Anybody that didn't have anything to do or was stranded or out of place, that's what they did with you. So they wouldn't take us up there. But we did get in through a village where they had just been through. And they had a post office in there. I'll never forget that. Mail strung all over everyplace. I look back, I should have grabbed a bunch of those letters and brought them back. Fifty years later you could look at them. But we just rode around there for a while and then went back and caught a ride back to the ship. That was my getting ashore in Okinawa.

sp.speaker: Zachary Miller
sp.p: Did you see any casualties or people that were injured?

sp.speaker: Arnold DeHeus
sp.p: There was -- I didn't see any up there. And we didn't really go with them all the time, but one of those fellows had gone out -- what they were doing was some kind of mop-up in these villages and checking them out again because the fighting had already moved on. So what we did -- he told us he had to kill somebody up there because they were in one of these buildings and they wear clothing that's not exactly like ours. A lot of it was robes and things. And some old guy, he was sitting -- He told us about it. He said he was sitting in the corner over there, and he reached for something, you know, maybe even put his hands down to get up or whatever. But he said he shot him because he didn't know for sure. And that's how it is.

So that's the closest I came to any of that, what you would call real action, because ours was not a fighting program but a material delivery program. But we were -- the kamikazes didn't discriminate. They'd take out civilians or anybody that was on that ship. The ships is what they were after. I think the battleships had so much armament they couldn't hardly get to them. It was almost like a lost cause to try to get to them. But when they did come over in those raids -- you wouldn't believe it, but if you had a panorama of it, the sky would just fill with tracers, lines going every which way. You would wonder what are they shooting at, because they are shooting and you don't see any planes over there. But you see ammunition going up -- or these tracers going up. And it was, well, bigger than 4th of July fireworks. It was just the whole sky, as far as we could see up and down, everybody was firing.

sp.speaker: Zachary Miller
sp.p: Let's talk about a bit of what your everyday life was like on the ship. Describe a typical day.

sp.speaker: Arnold DeHeus
sp.p: Well, the typical day would be -- it all depended on your rate, what you did. What I started out, the wipers were what they called day workers. We worked were eight to five. And a lot of times in the tropics when it was hot, we sometimes only worked from like a six-hour day.

The first engineer, who was your boss, would take pity on you because there was no air-conditioning on those ships. The only air-conditioning was to put a scoop out the porthole. If you were lucky enough to have a bunk by the porthole, that was okay. You would get a little breeze there. But it could also be an unlucky place to be because sometimes if you went to sleep there -- and this happened several times on ships I was on; fortunately I wasn't in that bunk -- but they would change course with the zigzagging I was telling you about. So you are going to get the sea or the waves coming from a different angle. And sometimes they are high enough they hit that scoop. And if you've ever been hit with one of those things, it's just like throwing a bathtub of water on your bunk. I mean, you come up right now, wide awake. And then everything is wet. It doesn't hurt the rooms any because they all have what they call scuppers in them. And there's a drain hole in them, even in the room, because it can take a wash down or whatever.

So that would be like an untypical day. In the tropics most of the time you just -- I think for months the only thing I wore was a pair of short Levis that we'd cut off to make shorts out of them. It was so hot. The engine room would be always a hundred degrees, maybe up to 120. I mean, it was -- it was hot down there. And the routine was -- if you weren't a wiper, then there was four on and eight off. So you had -- like the shift would be twelve to four. You worked twelve to four in the afternoon and midnight to four in the morning. And the others were broken up.

One ship I was on there was a junior engineer. The junior engineer got hurt, almost got washed over the side sounding the tanks. The fuel tanks, they keep track of how much fuel you were using, how much you had left and if you had to transfer fuel from one tank to another to maintain an even keel on it. And this wave came up, like one of those unusual ones, the seventh one or the seventeenth one, whatever it happens to be, and almost washed him overboard. But he got caught on the rail and hit his collarbone, like right here on the shoulder.

It saved him from going over, but it broke his collarbone. So he couldn't work, so the other junior and I had there worked six on and six off to cover for him. They don't carry any extra people. The crew was either well or somebody else has to pack the load. And if push came to shove, sometimes they would move somebody up. One time they had to take a pump man off of a ship I was on. And so, because I had been on tankers before, they moved the second pumpman up to first pumpman, and they moved me to second pumpman, out of order on that particular ship. That was a different ship than these others I was talking about, and it was after the war. We pulled into Sydney to offload -- Sydney, Australia, to offload cargo we picked up in the Gulf, Persian Gulf. And we couldn't go ashore.

Two young guys -- I think I was and the other chief pumpman was 20 years old. And as a pumpman, when you are offloading, has charge of everything. He tells them -- tells somebody what valves to open and close. Does everything. You don't have to do any like physical work. You had to go down and check the pumps every half hour or hour to make sure they are not running out of cargo. You can't let them run dry. But anyway, there's a system to it on what you have to do and your responsibilities.

Well, anyway the other guy and I -- young kids, again -- we couldn't go ashore because that was our work time. At sea we had all free time. There was nothing to do. Ride the ship till you get to port. So what you do in your free time is you play cards or you just get a suntan or lay around or make things, you know, do things that you can get on the ship. Anyway, when we pumped out this cargo in Sydney, we pumped that tanker out in three days -- no, no -- excuse me. hours. It wasn't three days. We pulled into -- we started -- we were there three days, but we pumped it dry in hours. That tanker, it's not like the big ones you see now, but it's a smaller one. I forget what it hauled. But they had 27 tanks on it. It really had nine tanks divided into three, and you could carry four or five different cargoes on it. But they had -- the pumps were, I think, ten by twelve pumps with a 200-horsepower electric motor on them that they would run. And so they moved some fuel in a hurry. And that's what we did. We kept them going. We even lined it up to run them down a lot lower than they recommended. And then you have a smaller pump you put on, what they call a stripping pump, and that takes out the bottom of it. So you get it right down to as low as you can go.

But I know that they were upset because they didn't get any time in Sydney, the crew. They said, "You guys" -- even the first mate was getting on us because we were running those big pumps, 200 horse, down to where they -- if they run out of product to pump, they start to vibrate. And they really vibrate. And we would get -- we would watch them and watch them. You could feel them even through the ship anyplace. If we'd just feel a little bit of vibration, we'd shut them off and put the strippers on them and work real fast and get that thing going so that was stripping while others were pumping or switch it over to pumping other cargo. That was -- Even the captain and those other guys couldn't believe that we did that. But young guys, you can go up and down these ladders and run around.

sp.speaker: Zachary Miller
sp.p: So you would work very hard to quickly unload the ship only to have no --

sp.speaker: Arnold DeHeus
sp.p: Yeah, because we didn't get any shore leave, we figured we wanted to get out of here.

sp.speaker: Zachary Miller
sp.p: Tell me about the food that you ate.

sp.speaker: Arnold DeHeus
sp.p: The food was -- wasn't bad. The food on there was different than that you would see in a -- I'd say a Navy ship or anything else because it was -- they still operate under union contract. You see, it was just like going on a job. You negotiated conditions. And one of the conditions was that somebody made your bed up every day and cleaned your room. And you had three men to a room usually in the quarter.

Like the three fireman slept together, the three oilers slept together. If you had junior engineers, they slept together in one room. So you had what you call a messman. And then every day -- or every week your linen was changed. And then in the tropics your pillow case was changed twice a week because you were perspiring all the time. And the food was -- you'd tell the messman what you wanted, and he would bring you a plate of this.

And then everything else was on the table. You sat at a regular dining table. It was about probably six men, maybe, to each side in there. And it wasn't crowded. The coffee pot was on all the time or the juices or whatever they had you could get anytime, whatever they had. We did not have much of that because they didn't have as big a setup. You're only talking forty men.

And the officers had their side, and the crew had the other side. So there was two separate mess halls, but we ate the same food. It all came from the same pot. Only one galley. Everybody ate out of that galley, officers and crew. The only difference was they had a little nicer dining area, but not any different, per se, than as the crew.

sp.speaker: Zachary Miller
sp.p: How did people entertain themselves? You said cards.

sp.speaker: Arnold DeHeus
sp.p: Yeah, they were playing a lot of cards and cribbage. One thing that we did do on my first trip, I remember, was when we got to Australia we picked up their coins. And the florin at that time was about the size of our 50 cent piece. You'd take this florin and hold it on edge, on davits (ph) back in the stern or whatever, sit down there on this thing. And it was heavy metals, and you'd take a spoon, regular tablespoon, and hit the edge of that coin until you flattened it out, until it was flat as a ring like this. That killed a lot of time. If you just take a coin and set it edge on and tap it with that spoon and see how far it goes -- you can't hardly see how far it goes. So that's what we would do to pass time.

We would go around and explore every nook and cranny of that ship, fore and aft, because for one thing it was something to do and then you wanted to see what you were sailing on. Another thing that I did is the way I learned to advance my rating, as a wiper I would go down after my day shift was over and I would go down in the evening to the engine room or the boiler room, and I would tell the fireman, "I want to learn how to do this fireman. I want to learn everything about it."

So you would trace out the steam lines, trace the lines wherever they go and what they did and operate it and why they did this and how they did it. And then I would physically do his job, clean -- you had to clean burners every watch. That's what the oil went through into the boiler and fires, if they had them, and it would build up carbon in there and they'd get dirty. So you had to clean those.

Well, I would clean his burners for him and I'd wipe things down. I'd take his readings for him. He would just there and make sure I was doing it right. And then they tell me everything about it. I would go up on top of the boiler -- even in this extremely hot weather, I would trace out these lines and see what was going on and analyze it. So you had everything to learn there. You had electrical distribution through the panel generating. You had refrigeration you could learn. Just pick everybody's brain on it so that -- because we had distilled water, sea water, so we would have fresh water. Learned about the bearings on the shaft, the big bearings they'd have. And it was just -- it was altogether a learning experience. It was like going to a special school.

And whatever you wanted to do you could do, from one end of the engine room to the other or top to bottom. And that's what I did. So when I left there, the endorsements I had -- we're going back to the lifeboat ticket was an endorsement, the fire and water tender, boiler, and then junior engineer. And that was as high as you could go in what they called unlicensed form. There you went to the officer range, the engineer.

sp.speaker: Zachary Miller
sp.p: Let's get back to talking about your experiences during the war. You left us, I believe, in -- last we talked in Australia unloading that tanker. This was in the wintertime of late '44, early '45?

sp.speaker: Arnold DeHeus
sp.p: Oh, yeah. That first ship I was on, Idaho Falls.

sp.speaker: Zachary Miller
sp.p: Actually, talk about the second ship, the Victory ship.

sp.speaker: Arnold DeHeus
sp.p: The Victory ship, I was on it for a short time. That's the one that just went from San Francisco and we sat in Okinawa and went back to San Francisco. And then I got off of it. And then -- So that would have been like July. And in July I caught -- I think I caught another ship there. That was probably the one -- I think that third ship I was on was one that was going to sail out of San Francisco, and they didn't know where it was going. And it sailed without me.

That was one of those -- And I was a fireman on that one. What had happened is I asked everybody, "When is this ship going to leave? When is it going to leave?" They are supposed to post a time that it's going to depart. So I had a girlfriend in Oakland, so I called her up and I said, "Well, this ship's not going to go until five or seven in the afternoon or evening" -- so this is like noon or something. I said, "Why don't you jump on the A train, come on over, we'll go to a movie or something here, and then I'll catch the ship." So she came over. And I was still like in my work clothes, my jeans and my T-shirt. It was a nice warm day. We walked up Market Street someplace there and took in a movie. And I was still asking all kinds of people, "When is this ship going to leave?" They all said, "Oh, yeah, it's going to leave at six o'clock, seven o'clock." So when I get back from the movie, no ship. I said, "Wait a minute. There's something wrong with this."

So I ran to the shipping office right away, which is a few blocks away, and told them, "I'm supposed to be on that ship over there." And usually what they do, if it's not too far out, they have a little boat, they run you out to that ship and you get on. Instead of that -- by the time I got there he said, "It just went under the Golden Gate, and it's too late." When you get past that Golden Gate and out there starting out, they have some awful currents out there. So they don't bother with trying to take boats out there and catching it. Kind of rough around those Farallones and that.

So all I could say was, you know, goodbye. And all my stuff and my gear was on there. I just bought all new gear and everything was on there. So I had to go down to the draft office because my time had been up. So I told them I missed the ship, and I told them why. I said, "They didn't post any notices. They told me all kinds of things, and then they took off."

So the lady there happened to be the mother of one of the kids I went to school with. So she knew me because I had seen him, and so she said, "Okay. I'll put it down here so you'll have to get another ship." So I caught another tanker real quick, and it was a coastal one. It was just going to run up and down the coast a little bit. So I said okay, so I took a fireman's job on that one. That was the JL Hannah, a Standard Oil tanker. So I think we made a trip up to Seattle and someplace there and then back down to L.A. or wherever it was. And then I got off of that and went back to Oakland because that ship was supposed to be back.
[END OF SIDE TWO, TAPE ONE; BEGIN SIDE ONE, TAPE TWO]

sp.speaker: Zachary Miller
sp.p: Before we go back to what we were talking about, in the break you mentioned that you had a kamikaze story.

sp.speaker: Arnold DeHeus
sp.p: Yeah. One of them was -- I was out watching this where we were tied up in the line, and it would be on the port side, which was facing ashore. And when I described it earlier about the anti-aircraft fire going up, I was on the side where you could watch the shore and the direction from which the kamikazes were coming. And I was watching all of these ships firing. Well, this one kamikaze that I think I told you or mentioned was coming towards our ship.

And our gunner was heading right straight for it. You could see his 20s going in there. Well, I don't know if it was that particular one or another one, but it was heading towards us. And it kept coming. It didn't go down. It kept coming. I says: He is going to make it. My brain says: He is going to make it.

So I went to the starboard side or the other side of the ship, which would have been like the ocean side. And I said: Well, if he hits, I'm going to be by this rail and it will probably knock me into the water and I'll have a chance. If I stay over there watching him and he hits, I might as well forget it because it would blow it up. So I went back there. I figured he is going to make it. So I went over there and I waited what I thought was an appropriate amount of time. And nothing happened. So I went back. And sure enough, he didn't make it. One of those gunners got him and he went down. But that was what you do. You don't have any way to fire back, so you start thinking of survival: How am I going to survive this? Well, that's what I did.

And then you think -- in this case, I wasn't in the engine room, but if he'd hit and I'd have been like in the engine room, that would be the end of you. Forget it. That pounds of steam and that 700 degree superheat, it would cook you.

So that was one of those experiences as close as I came to having any problem. One of those ships that was ahead of us -- when I came off of watch one morning, it was like I was on the twelve to four on that one. And so when I got off of watch and I came up on deck, sitting out there and everything was quiet -- when there's no battling, no firing, it's the quietest thing. You just can't imagine. The silence is deadening. It gets your attention.

All of a sudden there's a big explosion. Boom. I hear this thing and a big light. So I thought that the battleships up there, when they leave a shell in there, they don't leave it in, they fire it off, you know, no target or something. They don't try to take it out again; they fire it. So I thought that's what happened. So I went down with a big story. I said, yeah, told the guys down there, they just blew a ship up, you know. And come to find out later on how right I was.

The ship up ahead of us was another Merchant ship. And this kamikaze came in, one lone kamikaze, through all this undetected, probably flying low, and flew right into that cargo ship ahead of us and blew the whole bridge off that ship. Killed everybody. I think the one that survived was the third engineer, and he was down on watch. So this is what happens, how close it could be. That ship could just as easily have been our ship. And I would have been right there by the midsection where this plane hit. So somebody has their hand on your shoulder and guiding you.

Another experience I had is the kamikazes would sometimes, instead of coming in high, came in low. We had one come in low one time 20 foot off the water right down through the line of ships in there. I think he was trying to get to the battleships. And what happened is when they followed the plane and they get caught up in the -- to get the plane and concentrating on that, and the shells were going over and bouncing off the hull of another ship over there, so that's -- you could be killed by friendly fire.

Fortunately it was down on the lower part of the hull just above the water. But you could see them -- bam, bam, bam. So it's the hazards, even though you are not physically in all this battle, if you are over there in that area, what they call the hundred precent zone, you are susceptible to this all the time, air raids or submarines or whatever else. Mines. They had mines in those harbors and sea lanes that blow the ships up.

sp.speaker: Zachary Miller
sp.p: After the war ended, you continued on in your service in the Merchant Marines. Do you want it talk about other ships that you were on?

sp.speaker: Arnold DeHeus
sp.p: Oh, yeah. When the war was over, the President of the United States and the War Shipping Administration sent letters out to the Merchant seamen, one from the president, Truman, thanking us for sticking with it and delivering material and the effort that we put into the war. And the other was from the War Shipping Administration asking us to continue sailing because there was still a lot of work to do.

The supplies and equipment and everything had to be brought back, and also the troops had to be brought back. So I sailed on a couple of troop ships bringing them, the soldiers, back from Japan -- or the islands, I should say, wherever we picked them up. And they were -- sometimes it was a rough trip because they were jammed in there. And it was not a pleasant trip for them because they were stacked like six high in these bunks.

You had maybe 18 inches to two foot, max, between these bunks. They were stacked right in there like cord wood. And the facilities were such that for sanitary they just had open toilets in a big row for them to use because you couldn't have anything fancy down there. Most of them were just a trough. And they would wash this down with sea water all the time for urinals. And I don't think there was any showers on there. They just can -- because it was -- the odor was sometimes overpowering. And I know that a lot of those fellows would stay on deck, just stay on deck all the time. The only time they'd go down is to get something to eat. And if they went down there, they might put it in their mess kit and take it back up and eat on deck.

One time we hit some rough seas and the captain, over the loudspeakers, told everybody to get off the decks, inside. Some of them wouldn't get off then. I remember we took a big sea right over -- just aft of the bow, and it washed some of these guys back and forth. You could see them just washing back and forth on the deck. There's all kinds of obstructions on there. You have davits and you have other things you could tie off and things sticking up out of that deck.

Well, the next thing you know there's about two or three of them had to be stretchered off of there. I know one guy had a broken leg or something like that. It just sweeps you right -- your feet right off and throws you against the railings, like the fellow I was telling you about with the broken collarbone on there. But even that, those still toughed it out, even when they were on deck.

So anyway, one time one of them -- I don't think it was that same ship -- another one -- one of our officers died on the trip. That was the first time I had seen or experienced a death on the ship. And it was just from complications he had. He was an older fellow. I think he might have even been retired Navy, because we had a lot of retired Navy people serving in the Merchant Marine. They couldn't get back in the Navy, but they wanted to get in the war. He was buried at sea on this troop ship. That's the one I think I mentioned we had movies of that, all of them lined up on there and putting him over the side. So that was about the end of my real war experiences. The rest were experiences of still sailing.

sp.speaker: Zachary Miller
sp.p: Well, Benton wanted me to ask you a question. This is rewinding a bit to Pearl Harbor. What was the atmosphere like when you first got to Pearl Harbor? Was there a lot of anger felt?

sp.speaker: Arnold DeHeus
sp.p: Oh, I didn't -- I didn't sense any what you would call anger. I think the populists there -- I think a lot of the Hawaiian makeup is go with the flow, you know. I mean, it was -- it happened. There's nothing you can do about it. It's over with. You can't dwell on it forever. You have to go on with your life.

But there wasn't what I would call the sense of frivolity like it probably was before. You know, everything was vacation time, good time and partying. It was the place to go and to rest and relax. That part of it was gone. But as far as the Hawaiian people -- I wasn't really there long enough because that was that tanker that time, and tankers are not noted for staying long in port. So maybe one or two days is all you get.

I did get down to Waikiki Beach because that's what you heard about and saw in the movies. And at that particular time it was a big disappointment because there was rocks. When you tried to wade out in that -- I went swimming there just to say I had been swimming there. But there were rocks -- it wasn't all sandy. You would walk out and stub your toe on these rocks. They told me they cleaned all that out or hauled more sand in. But that was -- that was what I remembered -- probably one of the things that was kind of outstanding, how much they bragged about Waikiki Beach and all this. Well, it didn't impress me. Santa Cruz Beach was every bit as good.

sp.speaker: Zachary Miller
sp.p: What did you go on to do as a career after the war?

sp.speaker: Arnold DeHeus
sp.p: After the war -- well, I kept sailing -- Let's see. There was one other instance, if I might go back to that.

sp.speaker: Zachary Miller
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Arnold DeHeus
sp.p: That would be the delivery of a tanker to Cardiff, Wales on a Lend-Lease program to the British after the war. They needed ships. And we had a lot of tankers that weren't going to be doing much, I think, and a lot of other ships. So we did help them out. And we delivered this ship to Cardiff, Wales.

And I remember that as an unusual port because they have a high tide there -- I think there's only a few places in the world that have these high tides. The other one is Anchorage, Alaska. It's something like 30 feet. And when the tide is out, this little harbor, the boats sit right on the bottom. They have in there -- it's not there anymore, but at that time what they had there was what they called a graving dock.

Then you waited off -- off of the land out there until they signalled you that the tide was in at its highest. And then you went right in as fast as you could and you went right into these graving docks. And then they close those docks behind you, just like going through the canal or anything, and let the water drain out. And then your ship was sitting say high and dry in this graving dock. Then they could work on the hull or do whatever they had to to.

Well, we delivered this tanker there to the English on this Lend-Lease. And I remember when we shut it down, there isn't anything more depressing or scary than a ship with no lights on anyplace and no electricity, no -- one of those big ships. And it's dark down in there and cold. There's no heat, no anything.

And this would be in probably the latter part of 1947 -- yeah, latter part of 47. And so what we did, we had all our supplies on there. And I remember that they said, "Well, you can take anything you want on here." They were on a metric system, even though ours -- we had tools and everything. So I took a little flaring tool that I've still got off that ship in '47. And then I took a great big ham, frozen ham. It had to weigh 20 pounds if it weighed an ounce. I said, "This is going to be our entertainment for the evening."

So I took that ham. And they had to furnish us a place to stay, you know, while we were waiting for transportation to London. So I took the ham, and I went to -- I picked out a nice pub I liked. And two or three of my buddies and I went in there. And I put that ham on the bar. And I talked to the bartender a little bit and asked him things like how much he thought that ham was worth. It was worth a lot. He said, "I couldn't afford that ham." Well, I says, "How about we do this, you just keep the drinks coming until you figured we paid for that ham." We stayed there, partied all night long on that ham. And we were happy and he was happy. I'll never forget that. And all those guys told me, "Why are you taking that?" I said, "I've got something in mind for that." So that's what it was.

They took us down to London. And of course our contract called for first class accommodations and transportation if they had to transport us anyplace. And so we got to the shipping agent in London. And there were three ships delivered at this same time approximately. Not all into Wales. Some went to other places, but we all happened to meet at this one shipping agent's office to get accommodations someplace. Well, he was going to stick us way out of town or out of the city in a cold water flat out there someplace. And we said, "Well, we're not going to go for that because we want first class."

And I happened to be a delegate, a union delegate, for the engine room on that ship. So anyway, we got our heads together. And the one crew that was there, they said, "Well, we'll take it because we are going to leave tomorrow." They were only going to stay one day, and we were farther behind. We had to stay for a couple of days to wait for transportation. So they said, "We'll go out and take it and call you back and let you know about the situation." So that's what they did. And they said, "Don't take this thing." That's how we found out what it was, you know, nothing out there. But they was going to put up with it for one night.

So we held fast for first class. And the shipping agent didn't want to give us anything. He wanted to send us out there. I said, "Okay. We'll stay right here in this office. We're not going to move. We'll stay right here in this office. Either we get first class accommodations or we'll stay right here all night long." So where did they put us up? In Regent's Palace right down in Piccadilly Circus. That's the only first class he could get. So here we are, typical dress-up outfit, engineer boots, Levis and bomber jacket -- and T-shirt. And we're in this place.

And I'll never forget that. There wasn't any private baths. You had to go to the hall. But they had a little pitcher and bowl in the room and nice rooms. And when we went down to dinner, there was about four of us or so, kind of buddies there. We went down to eat dinner. And here comes the waiter in a tux. And he has a towel draped over his arm. And there's about a six-piece string orchestra. We were there -- I think there was one other couple in there or something, but we was the only ones in there. So we had the whole thing to ourselves. And anyway, we had a nice dinner there. And it felt a little bit out of place, but I thought, what the heck, we just fought a war, you know. So we put up with it. It was nice.

And then went to a dance. They had the Lyceum dance hall, which is a rather large dance hall only a few blocks away. I think I still have that membership card. The only way you could get in there is if you were a member. So we bought a membership card and then went in there to dance because all of this -- sailors like to dance. And it had a sloping dance floor, if you could believe that, up to a stage. It wasn't very much, but it was a slope. And of course they went around, so you would dance uphill and then you'd dance downhill. You could go around like this. I'll never forget that.

What we did while we were there we had extra time, and rather than hit all the bars, I went to places like the Parliament building, London Bridge. I saw London Bridge before they moved it to Arizona, you know, and went across in its original spot, and Trafalgar Square. So we went around to look at what was there that's going to last. And that was another experience that I had. And then I had -- when we came back, rather than -- you could take a ship, a liner, or you could fly. I flew back on one of those old three-tail Connies. The rest of the crew -- not all the crew -- I don't know how many, but some took the ship. The captain took the liner back. He wouldn't fly. So anyway, that had to be first class.

Well, first class at that time it was all the drinks you could stand. And it was a 13-hour trip. Well, young guys, you could go all night long and the next day, too. But anyway, it was kind of a fun trip. Then they had to put us up in New York until the captain got back. And he was taking the ship. So that was a week before he would get back over to New York. So we stayed -- I've still got the tag off of that -- the Forest Hotel right off Times Square. And Madison Square Garden and Jack Dempsey's Bar was right across, kitty-corner on the street. Roseland Ballroom. And that was in -- right about New Year's of '47 or that week between Christmas and New Year's.

And I think it was just before New Year's they had the biggest snowstorm ever blow in for the last 50 years or something and shut Times Square down. We only had to walk like maybe -- I would say 200 feet or something to get to Broadway. And look down there, there wasn't a soul around. No cars. No anything. It was just quiet. If you could imagine New York. I think they've had as big a snowstorm since then, but that was the biggest one they'd had then. So anyway I spent New Year's, '47 and '48 in that Roseland Ballroom.

sp.speaker: Zachary Miller
sp.p: Let's talk about what you did after the war. How did you make it back up to Alaska? What were the circumstances?

sp.speaker: Arnold DeHeus
sp.p: After the war I went back to Oakland again. At that time I traveled from New Orleans. I'd paid off my last ship in New Orleans and went back to Oakland. And my sister was there. And she said, "You better go see your folks," because I hadn't seen my folks since 1941 when I went to that, seven years, 1948.

So here I -- they got older, and I had transformed from a kid to a man, you know, by that time. So I came back up here to Alaska on a visit. I had a round trip plane ticket out of San Francisco to Fairbanks. And at that time you had to stop at White Horse and refuel in Canada because the planes weren't equipped or qualified to fly over water. So you had to stick with the land route. Anyway, I got here.

And my sister wanted to come up, so I said, "Well, okay." She was going to come up a couple of weeks after me. I said, "Well, okay, I'll see if I can get your air fare together to go over and see my mother," who was in Rampart. So I went to work in a butcher shop cutting up -- it was in the fall of the year. I came up like August or something, and moose meat was coming in. So I was working there to make some money to give her to have a ticket. Well, I was eating moose steaks for a while there because there's always some waste, you know, cutting them up. But anyway, that was my experience with meat cutting, so I learned a little bit about meat cutting there.

Then I got a job with the FE Company. This is where my mechanical training paid off because they needed a pipe fitter, plumber over there. And so my dad knew all the -- most of the people that worked there because he worked for the mining company for about ten years or 15 years, something like that. So I went over there. And the foreman asked me, he said, "Do you know how to put a thread on the end of a pipe?" "Yeah," I said, "I can do that." "Okay," he said, "you're hired." So I was the only pipe fitter they had or plumber. And they gave me a truck, and I did maintenance in all the camps around here. There was at Fox and out at Chataneeka (ph), Long Creek, Cripple Creek, and did some maintenance work on the dredges when they were working. Dredge 8 out there that they are advertising here, I had to change some piping out there one time. Anyway, I spent a couple of years there. And my Marine training had paid off.

Then I -- the folks were in mining all the time, so I -- they talked me into spending one season with them mining. That's the hardest work I ever did in my life. I had a bellyful of mining after that first -- and we only were mining, actual mining it, for about, I would say six weeks or something like that. But they kind of broke even or made expenses, but we never got rich on it. So -- I did make a mistake.

They told me they would pay me off in gold or, for the season, $2,000. Well, I took the $2,000, and I should have taken the gold because gold went from $35 an ounce at that time to, what, it jumped almost to $700 a few years later, you know. But money was -- I guess that's all kids knew. I'll take the money. So then --

sp.speaker: Zachary Miller
sp.p: I just want to say that we only have a little bit of time left.

sp.speaker: Arnold DeHeus
sp.p: Oh. So then I went to -- when I came back, I went to work in the power plants again. I worked at the old power plant at the old Ladd Field down in the main area. And I worked there for a while. And then they built the new city plant, at that time, in 1951 over here on the river. And the chief engineer at that Ladd Field plant went over to start that one up.

He was an old Merchant Marine man, so I asked him, "How about me going over with you?" He said, "Okay. I can't make you an engineer, but you can start as fireman." I started as fireman again, only it was coal instead of oil. So I fired for about two months over there. And then one of those engineers quit because it was all new, modern stuff and he couldn't pick it up. And it was easy for me. So he moved me in as engineer. And I worked there for a couple of years. And then they started the plant at Isleson at that time. And he went to the Isleson plant, the chief. So I said, "I'll go with you, if that's okay."

So I went with him out there. And they needed test engineers to test it. So I was a test engineer for a while, and then I went back to operating engineer after the test was over. Then from that one I quit that job because I was making the least amount of money and I was breaking in about 15 men on their different jobs they had to do. They were all making more money than I was. I thought there's something wrong with that picture there. So I left there and ended up at the university up here, the assistant chief engineer with another one guy that had been engineer at Isleson.

So I worked there for several years and then finally decided that I didn't want to be tied down to a power plant or engineer. I wanted to build things. So I went into the plumbers and pipe fitters local in 1956 and been there ever since. Almost got 50 years with them. And held most every office in there. Past president of the local plumbers and pipe fitters. So that's -- My trade worked out good. I had just as good a life there. In fact, I had a pretty good life all the way through.

sp.speaker: Zachary Miller
sp.p: Is there anything that you would like to add that we may not have covered in the interview, a totally different subject maybe, before we finish?

sp.speaker: Arnold DeHeus
sp.p: This's one subject that I am kind of hip on is the lack of patriotism and U.S. history taught to the students in this country. The people don't seem to have the same -- I don't know if you would call it dedication, esprit de corps, the honor of having a country like America to live in.

I can't believe that the people that enjoy all the privileges we have can go out and protest in favor of, an example, a dictator that persecutes his population. There's something that doesn't jibe in my brain with something like that after serving in a war to save this country for freedom.

Freedom is -- really, you don't have freedom. You have freedom within balance. You don't have freedom if everything is out of balance. You can't do that. Everybody can't go do their own thing helter skelter because you have to have some kind of cohesiveness and things to progress and develop and to remain strong. If you don't have that, you might as well give it up. Freedom is the main thing. And it seems like we have it, but we relinquish a lot of it too easy.

The government shouldn't be telling you when to get up, when to go to bed, what you are going to eat, what you can do, what you can't do. Freedom. Freedom is using your imagination and your abilities to develop the country and promote it and not -- not try to tear it down. I can't understand that. It's like destroying your own home.

They call it something different, like messing in your nest. But this is one of the things that when I was growing up here and going to school, it was pledge of allegiance every day. And they were strict. You had rules to live by here, a code of the North. And that's what you lived by. You helped other people; people helped you. You got along, even though you had fights and arguments. Like this bullying business, yeah, every school -- every kid went to school, they had a bully there someplace. Well, pretty soon he gets tired of beating on you or else you get together and you show him what happens when you beat on somebody. And that solves all that problem.
But there's no -- there's no respect, the way I see it. Everything is do your own thing, no matter who it affects or what it affects or how it affects you. And I just I hope the cycle...
END OF SIDE ONE, TAPE TWO; BEGIN SIDE TWO, TAPE TWO

sp.speaker: Zachary Miller
sp.p: We were talking about how you felt about --

sp.speaker: Arnold DeHeus
sp.p: Yeah. And I think the other thing is education. We have to go start insisting that if you are going to have the education and if you are going to go through school and if you are going to get your diploma, you are going to have to do it right. Close enough is not going to be good enough.

I can't imagine -- I was amazed in World War II when somebody got on the ship from San Francisco and couldn't read the bulletin board. There he is, 17 years old, and he couldn't read. We finally found out because we'd tell him, "Go read this." Finally one day he had to fess up: "I can't read."

I thought that at that time, I can't imagine somebody can't read in this country. Well, now here it is, what, over 50 years later and we still have people that can't read. We've got to teach them how to read. There's something wrong with it. There's something wrong someplace. And money is not going to solve it. It has to be mom and pop teaching the kids, the school teaching the kids. And I mean not putting up with kids. What they do, they put up with them, let them run loose let them do their thing. The thing is you've got to teach them. You don't want to put up with them. I think the country has to cycle back into that type of a thing. Educate them properly and right and with some patriotism.

sp.speaker: Zachary Miller
sp.p: Okay. Well, I would just like to say for the record that this has been an interview with Arnold DeHeus. I want to say thank you on behalf of myself, Benton, and I think I can speak for Jason, for your service to our country. It's for the sacrifices that people like yourself have made that we can enjoy those freedoms you are talking about. And thank you. Just for, I guess, secretarial duties, this is my tape 06.0 -- no -- 03.06. We have been sitting with Arnold DeHeus. Today's date is June the 3rd, 2003. And Benton Widyard (ph) and Jason DeHeus and myself were the only other three people in the room. Thank you very much, Arnold.

sp.speaker: Arnold DeHeus
sp.p: Thank you.
[END OF INTERVIEW]
